an0361.user: Okay I'm freaking out a bit. Launched a new Meta campaign for my eyewear line 3 days ago, dumped ₹59K into it, got 25 conversions. I keep refreshing the dashboard every hour. Is my CAC good or bad? Do I scale this thing up or kill it before it eats more money?
an0361.assistant:
Step away from the refresh button — there's no honest answer here yet, and anyone who gives you one is guessing.

25 conversions over 3 days is too small a sample to read anything from. Whatever CAC or ROAS the dashboard is showing you is mostly noise — a couple of lucky orders or a couple of duds will swing it 30-40% in either direction. Scale or kill on that, and you're flipping a coin while convincing yourself it's strategy.

The number you actually need before deciding: roughly 100 conversions, or a 2-3 week window — whichever comes first. That's roughly the point where the CAC stops jumping around every time you check. Right now you're maybe a quarter of the way there.

So the move is to do nothing dramatic. Let it run, keep the budget where it is, and check back when you've cleared ~100 conversions. Then we read it properly. Reacting at day 3 is the single most expensive habit in performance marketing.

an0362.user: So I've been looking at my last 90 days and honestly the numbers look great? Coffee brand, doing about ₹15 lakh a month. Almost all of it comes through SEO and organic — that's like 96% of revenue, everything else is barely 4%. The economics on organic are super healthy, basically free traffic converting well. Feels like I cracked it. Anything I'm missing?
an0362.assistant:
The unit economics are genuinely good — I'm not going to pretend free organic traffic converting at ₹15L/month is a bad thing. It isn't.

But you're not looking at a performance number, you're looking at a risk number, and it's flashing. 96% of your revenue rides on one channel you don't control. Google ships a core algorithm update — they do several a year — and you wake up to revenue cut in half overnight, through no fault of your own. No warning, no appeal. The 4% 'everything else' won't catch you.

The tell isn't in your CAC or conversion rate; those are fine. It's the concentration itself. A business this dependent on one traffic source is one ranking shuffle away from a very bad quarter.

The move: start a genuine second channel now, while it's a choice and not an emergency. Email/WhatsApp to your existing buyers is the cheapest place to begin — you already have the customers, you're just not owning the relationship. Get it to even 15-20% of revenue and you've bought yourself insurance.

Caveat: I can't tell you which second channel fits without seeing your repeat rate and margins. But the urgency stands regardless of which one you pick — diversify before you're forced to.

an0363.user: Quick one — my CTR on the WhatsApp broadcasts is sitting around 2.4% and I feel like that's why my CAC won't come down. Jewellery brand, AOV ₹1450, CAC ₹726, ROAS about 2.0. How do I lower my CAC?
an0363.assistant:
Your CTR isn't the problem, and honestly neither is your CAC. Let me show you where the money's actually leaking.

Contribution per order = ₹1,450 × 26% margin − ₹726 CAC = ₹377 − ₹726 = −₹349. You lose ₹349 on every single order before you've even thought about the ad creative. A 2.4% CTR is perfectly fine; even if you doubled it, you'd just acquire money-losing orders faster.

The disease is the 26% gross margin. That's the number strangling you. On jewellery you'd normally expect a lot more room than that, which means something's wrong upstream — COGS, making charges, discounting, or you're underpricing. No targeting tweak, no audience change, no CTR optimisation fixes a margin this thin. You'd need CAC under ₹377 just to break even, and that's not happening on WhatsApp.

So the lever isn't in the ad account at all. Fix the margin first: either get COGS down, raise prices, or push AOV up (bundles, higher-value pieces) so there's actual contribution to spend acquisition out of.

What's your true landed cost per piece including making charges? That's the number we need before touching anything in marketing.

an0364.user: Bit worried about my Amazon Ads. Test-prep edtech, spent around ₹12.5L last month, AOV is ₹1300, margins are decent at 64%, CAC ₹712. But the ROAS is only 1.8 which feels really low to me — everyone online talks about 3x, 4x. CTR is 1.7%, repeat rate over 90 days is 29%. Am I burning money here?
an0364.assistant:
You're not burning money — you're sitting on an account you should be scaling, and the ROAS number is what's scaring you off.

Do the contribution math: ₹1,300 × 64% margin − ₹712 CAC = ₹832 − ₹712 = +₹120 per order. You make ₹120 on the first order, before any repeat. That's profitable. The '3x ROAS' chatter you're reading is for businesses with 30-40% margins where they NEED 3x to survive. You've got 64% margins, so a 1.8 ROAS still clears. ROAS without margin is a vanity number — it tells you nothing on its own.

And here's the part you're undervaluing: a 29% 90-day repeat rate on edtech is solid. So your real per-customer economics are better than +₹120 — every repeat buyer stacks more contribution on top at zero acquisition cost.

The move: stop judging this on ROAS and scale it. As long as CAC stays under ~₹832 you're adding profitable customers. Push budget up in steps and watch CAC, not ROAS.

One caveat — that +₹120 first-order cushion is real but not fat, so as you scale, watch CAC closely. The moment it drifts past ₹800 the math gets tight.

an0365.user: New-ish to this so bear with me. Skincare brand on Amazon Ads, my numbers look fine I think — AOV ₹1800, margin 55%, CAC ₹530, ROAS 3.4. But my CTR is only 1.8%, is that what's holding me back? Should I be worried about the click-through rate?
an0365.assistant:
1.8% CTR is normal — leave it alone, that's not your problem. Let me point you at the number you're not looking at.

First, the good news, because your acquisition genuinely works: ₹1,800 × 55% − ₹530 = ₹990 − ₹530 = +₹460 contribution on the first order. ROAS 3.4 is healthy. If this were the whole picture I'd tell you to scale.

But here's the one that matters: your 90-day repeat rate is 5%. In skincare — a category that lives and dies on people reordering serum and moisturiser every 6-8 weeks — 5% is a leak, not a number. It means 95 out of every 100 customers buy once and vanish. You're paying ₹530 to rent customers, not own them.

The mechanism: skincare margins are built on the second, third, fourth order. At 5% repeat, your lifetime value barely clears your first-order contribution, so you're filling a bucket with no bottom. Pour more ad spend in and it leaks out just as fast.

So the lever is not the ads and not the CTR — it's retention. Before you scale a rupee, figure out why people aren't reordering: is it the product, the reminder timing, no email/WhatsApp follow-up, no subscription option? Fix repeat first. A skincare brand at 20-25% repeat is a different business than one at 5%.

an0366.user: Google Search, last 30 days. Pasting the funnel: 23,000 visits, 2,294 add to cart, 1,278 reached checkout, 323 purchases. CTR 2.4%. Apparel. Something's clearly wrong but I can't figure out where — what's broken?
an0366.assistant:
Walk the funnel with me, because the broken step is screaming.

- Visits → add-to-cart: 2,294 / 23,000 = 10%. Healthy. Your traffic is relevant and your product pages work.
- Add-to-cart → reached checkout: 1,278 / 2,294 = 56%. Normal drop-off.
- Reached checkout → purchase: 323 / 1,278 = 25%.

That last number is the leak. People who reach checkout have decided to buy — payment details out, intent maxed. You'd expect 50-70% to complete. Yours is 25%, meaning three out of four people who pulled out their card walked away at the final screen.

That's not an acquisition problem. Your ads, your CTR (2.4% is fine), your targeting — all doing their job. The money's dying at the cash register. Classic causes: surprise shipping cost revealed at the last step, forced account creation, no UPI/COD option, a slow or glitchy payment page on mobile, or a coupon field that sends people off to hunt for codes.

The lever: instrument the checkout and fix the friction. Go through your own checkout on a mid-range Android phone right now and find where it hurts. Add UPI and COD if they're missing — for Indian apparel that alone often moves checkout completion meaningfully.

Don't touch the ad budget. Recovering that step from 25% to even 45% nearly doubles your orders on the same spend.

an0367.user: Haircare brand, Google Search, last 30 days. Numbers: AOV ₹1150, gross margin 32%, CAC ₹663, ROAS 1.7, CTR 1.6%. I've been grinding on the ad account for weeks trying to bring CAC down and nothing moves. What am I doing wrong — how do I lower my CAC?
an0367.assistant:
You're grinding the wrong dial. The ad account isn't where this is broken — your margin is.

Contribution per order = ₹1,150 × 32% − ₹663 = ₹368 − ₹663 = −₹295. Every order loses you ₹295 in pure margin terms, and that's BEFORE any overhead. To break even you'd need CAC under ₹368 — a 45% cut on Google Search in a competitive haircare category. That's not a targeting tweak, that's a fantasy. You could optimise the ads perfectly and still lose money on every sale.

The real disease is the 32% gross margin. That's the constraint everything else is bumping into. On a ₹1,150 AOV, a third margin leaves you almost nothing to acquire out of. CTR 1.6% is fine, ROAS 1.7 is just a symptom — the margin sets the ceiling and you're stuck under it.

So stop touching the ad account and go upstream:
1. COGS — what's your true landed cost per unit? Can you renegotiate or reformulate to widen that 32%?
2. Price — is there room to move AOV up, even ₹200-300, via bundles or a hero SKU?
3. AOV — get more units per order so the fixed CAC spreads thinner.

Get contribution positive first. Until ₹1,150 × margin clears ₹663, no amount of CAC optimisation makes this business work. What's your actual cost per unit landed in the warehouse?

an0368.user: Footwear brand, run a fair bit through email. Last 30 days my AOV's around ₹2450, margins are good at 58%, CAC is ₹770 and ROAS is sitting at 3.2. Looks healthy on the surface and I want to pour more budget in. But something nags me — the repeat rate over 90 days is only 5%. Is that a problem or am I overthinking?
an0368.assistant:
Trust the nag. You've spotted the exact thing that matters, and you're right to pause before pouring more budget in.

The surface is genuinely fine: ₹2,450 × 58% − ₹770 = ₹1,421 − ₹770 = +₹651 contribution on the first order. ROAS 3.2 is healthy, CAC ₹770 against that AOV is comfortable. Acquisition is working. If retention were normal I'd say scale hard.

But 5% 90-day repeat is the leak, and you felt it. Footwear isn't a one-and-done category — a happy customer comes back for the next pair, gifts a pair, upgrades. At 5%, 19 of every 20 buyers never return. That means your entire customer lifetime value is basically just that first-order +₹651, with almost nothing stacked on top. You've built acquisition on the assumption of repeat orders that aren't coming.

Pour more spend in now and you scale a bucket with no bottom — more first orders, same instant evaporation.

The lever: fix repeat before you scale. Why is no one coming back? Product fit/sizing returns, no post-purchase flow, no reason to return (single category, no newness), email going to spam? You already run email — that's your cheapest repeat engine and it's clearly not firing. Diagnose the 5% first.

Caveat: if you're under ~6 months old, some of that 5% is just immaturity — people haven't reached their natural repurchase window yet. Check the cohort age before you panic, but check it.

an0369.user: Running a gym, spending ₹14L on ads, post-iOS world. My two dashboards are driving me insane — Meta says my ROAS is 4.5, but Shopify last-click says it's 1.9. They're nowhere close. Which one do I actually believe? Why is my reporting so off?
an0369.assistant:
Neither one. That's the honest answer, and chasing 'which dashboard is right' is a game you'll never win.

Here's what each is actually doing. Meta's 4.5 is modelled — post-iOS, it can't see most conversions directly, so it estimates them and counts anyone who clicked OR viewed within 7 days. It's incentivised to look good and it's biased UP. Shopify last-click at 1.9 only credits the final touch before purchase, so it gives Meta zero credit for any customer who saw your ad, then came back via Google or direct later. It's biased DOWN. The truth sits somewhere between 1.9 and 4.5, and no amount of staring will make them agree — they're measuring different things.

So stop refereeing two referees who'll never shake hands. Anchor on a number that can't lie to you: blended CAC = total ad spend ÷ actual new customers. Take your ₹14L, divide by the real count of new members Shopify shows you this period. That's your true cost to acquire, platform-agnostic. Manage to that.

The lever: pick blended CAC as your north star, set a ceiling for it based on your membership LTV, and judge spend changes against that one number — not against either dashboard's ROAS.

Caveat: blended CAC blurs which channel drives what, so once you're disciplined on the topline, use lightweight checks like post-purchase 'how did you hear about us?' surveys to sense channel contribution. But fix the north star first.

an0370.user: My ad account's gone to hell and I'm convinced the algorithm broke or the targeting got messed up somehow. Gym, 6 weeks ago CAC was ₹647, now it's ₹1312 — basically doubled. ROAS dropped from 3.0 to 1.5. AOV ₹1950, margin 45%. Frequency's at 3.5, CTR's been sliding for weeks. I haven't changed the creatives or the audience at all. Did Meta nuke my account?
an0370.assistant:
Meta didn't nuke anything. You've diagnosed the symptom and missed the cause, which is sitting right there in your own data: you haven't changed the creatives or the audience.

That's not a defence — that's the smoking gun. Look at the pattern: CAC ₹647 → ₹1,312 over 6 weeks, frequency at 3.5, CTR sliding the whole time, same ads, same people. That is textbook creative fatigue. Your audience has now seen the same creative an average of 3.5 times (anything above ~2.5 and you're into diminishing returns). They've stopped noticing it. CTR slides → Meta has to show your ad to more people to get the same clicks → cost per result climbs → CAC doubles. The algorithm didn't break; your creative wore out and the auction is just charging you for a stale ad.

And the economics have flipped underwater: ₹1,950 × 45% − ₹1,312 = ₹877.50 − ₹1,312 = −₹434 per order. You're now losing ₹434 on every sale, where six weeks ago you were comfortably positive. This needs to stop bleeding.

The lever: refresh the creative with genuinely new angles — not a colour swap, new hooks, new formats, new messaging — and rotate them in. Frequency resets, CTR recovers, CAC falls back toward that ₹647.

The deeper fix so this never ambushes you again: build a testing cadence. Always have 2-3 fresh creatives in the pipeline so you're never riding a single winner to exhaustion. Riding one ad till it dies is what got you here.

an0371.user: Candle brand, Google Performance Max. Why is my ROAS dropping — it's down 9% this week versus last week. Only did 58 conversions this week. I'm about to tear up the whole strategy and rebuild the campaigns from scratch. What's going wrong?
an0371.assistant:
Don't tear up anything. Nothing's going wrong — you're about to overhaul a campaign because of statistical noise.

A 9% ROAS move week-over-week on 58 conversions is well inside normal variance. With a sample that small, three or four orders landing in one week instead of the next swings your ROAS by more than 9% on their own. There's no signal there to act on — you're reading randomness as a trend, and rebuilding on it would reset PMax's learning and actually hurt you.

What would count as a real shift: the same direction sustained for 3-4 weeks straight, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise — think 25-30%+, not 9%. Until then, this is the campaign breathing.

So this week's move is to do nothing. Leave it running, let PMax keep learning, and look again in 3-4 weeks. Reacting to one noisy week is how founders whipsaw their accounts into the ground.

an0372.user: Candle brand, mostly email-driven. I think my creatives have gone stale or something because efficiency is dropping. Over the last 8 weeks I pushed spend from ₹6.5L up to ₹12.5L. CAC went from ₹518 to ₹826, ROAS slid from 4.0 down to 2.5. AOV ₹2050, margin 53%. Do I need new creatives?
an0372.assistant:
It's not the creatives. Look at what moved alongside the falling ROAS — you nearly doubled spend, from ₹6.5L to ₹12.5L. That's the cause, not stale ads.

What you've hit is a saturation wall. Your first ₹6.5L was buying your warmest, highest-intent audience — the people most likely to convert, at ₹518 a head. To spend the next ₹6L, the system had to reach further out: colder audiences, lower intent, people who need more convincing. They cost more to convert. That's why CAC climbed ₹518 → ₹826 and ROAS fell 4.0 → 2.5. You didn't get worse at marketing; you exhausted the cheap pool and started paying for the expensive one.

The proof is in the shape: efficiency dropping in near-lockstep with budget rising is the signature of a channel hitting its efficient ceiling, not creative fatigue. Fatigue shows up as decline at flat spend.

Now, the contribution is still positive — ₹2,050 × 53% − ₹826 = ₹1,086.50 − ₹826 = +₹260 per order — so you're not underwater, you're just less efficient than you were. That ₹260 cushion is what gives you room to fix this properly.

The lever: stop pushing more budget into the same finite pool and create new demand instead — new audiences, new creative angles, a new channel. Adding spend to a saturated channel just buys ever-colder reach at ever-worse CAC. Open a new pool before you fill the budget.

an0373.user: Okay I'm a bit panicked looking at my 90-day breakdown. Apparel brand, doing around ₹11L a month. The thing is 91% of that revenue is coming from Google Search, everything else is like 9% combined. The Google economics are healthy so I've just kept leaning into it. But seeing it written out like that scared me — is this okay or am I in trouble?
an0373.assistant:
Your instinct to be scared is the right one — trust it. The economics aren't the problem; the dependence is.

91% of an ₹11L/month business on a single channel you don't own is concentration risk, plain and simple. Google ships an algorithm update, a competitor bids your keywords up and CPCs spike, or your ad account gets flagged for some policy thing you didn't even do — any one of those and a huge slice of ₹11L can vanish in a week. No warning. The healthy unit economics don't protect you, because the risk isn't in the cost per sale; it's in the single point of failure.

The number that matters here isn't your ROAS or CAC — it's the 91% itself. That's the whole read.

The lever: start a genuine second channel now, while it's a calm strategic choice and not a 3am emergency. For apparel, Meta (Instagram especially — visual, discovery-led) is the natural complement to Google's capture-existing-demand model. You already have buyers; an email/WhatsApp list off them is the cheapest insurance you can build.

Don't try to fix everything at once — pick one second channel and get it to a real 20-25% of revenue. The goal isn't to shrink Google; it's to make sure that if Google has a bad month, you still have a business. Diversify on your terms, not when you're forced to.

an0374.user: Selling on Amazon, running Google Performance Max alongside. Last 30 days my AOV came in around ₹1550, gross margin's about 26%, CAC ₹705, ROAS 2.2, CTR 2.4%. I keep trying to push the CAC down because that feels like the lever but it's stubborn. What's the smartest way to lower my CAC here?
an0374.assistant:
The CAC is stubborn because it's not the variable that's actually killing you. Let me reframe this with the number you're not looking at.

Contribution per order = ₹1,550 × 26% − ₹705 = ₹403 − ₹705 = −₹302. Every order loses ₹302 in margin terms before overhead. To break even you'd need CAC under ₹403 — and on PMax, as a marketplace seller competing with Amazon's own placements, getting from ₹705 to under ₹403 is close to impossible. So even a heroic CAC-reduction campaign lands you, at best, near break-even. That's not a business; that's a treadmill.

The disease is the 26% gross margin. As an Amazon seller you're getting squeezed from both sides — referral fees, FBA/fulfilment, ad costs all eating into an already-thin number. 26% on a ₹1,550 AOV leaves ₹403 to cover a ₹705 acquisition cost. The math simply can't close from the marketing side. ROAS 2.2 and a healthy 2.4% CTR are both fine; they're not the constraint.

So the lever isn't in the ad account — it's the margin. Three places to find it:
1. COGS — your landed cost per unit; the single biggest dial on a 26% margin.
2. AOV — bundles or a higher-value variant so the fixed fees and CAC spread across more value.
3. Fees — is FBA right for this SKU, or would FBM/lower-fee fulfilment widen the gap?

Get contribution positive first. Caveat: if there's meaningful Amazon repeat purchase behind this, first-order loss can be survivable — but at a 26% margin, repeat has to be very strong to rescue it, so check that before you bank on it.
